content: Extremely premature infants are at risk of developing transient hypothyroxinaemia during the first weeks of life. This condition is characterized by low levels of thyroid hormones, which have been associated with an increased risk of neonatal complications, higher mortality rates, and long-term developmental impairments. It has been hypothesized that thyroid hormone therapy could potentially mitigate these adverse outcomes. The objective of this review was to evaluate the evidence regarding the use of thyroid hormone therapy in preterm infants with transient hypothyroxinaemia, specifically to determine whether it improves neonatal outcomes and neurodevelopment. Transient hypothyroxinaemia in this context is defined as low thyroid hormone levels with normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels. To address this question, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, PREMEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to March 2006. Additional sources, such as previous reviews, conference proceedings, and expert informants, were also consulted. The inclusion criteria required randomized or quasi-randomized trials involving preterm infants with transient hypothyroxinaemia, comparing thyroid hormone therapy to a control group (placebo or no treatment). The data collection and analysis process involved independent assessments of trial quality and data extraction by the review authors. The results were synthesized using standard Cochrane methods, including the calculation of relative risk (RR) and weighted mean difference (WMD). Only one study met the inclusion criteria. This study, conducted by Chowdhry in 1984, included 23 preterm infants weighing less than 1250 grams and born at 25 to 28 weeks of gestation. These infants had transient hypothyroxinaemia, defined as serum total T4 levels ≤ 4 μg/dL and TSH levels ≤ 20 IU/L. The infants were randomized to receive either thyroxine at a dose of 10 μg/kg/day or a placebo, starting on day 15 of life and continuing daily for seven weeks. The study reported no neonatal mortality in either group, with one infant death in each group prior to discharge. There were no significant differences between the thyroxine and placebo groups in terms of chronic lung disease (CLD) at 28 days or 36 weeks, patent ductus arteriosus, necrotizing enterocolitis, retinopathy of prematurity, weight gain, head circumference growth, or length growth. Additionally, there was no significant difference in mean T4 levels between the two groups on days 21, 35, 49, 63, and 77 after birth. Free T4 levels were not measured in this study. Neurodevelopmental follow-up was insufficient to draw any meaningful conclusions. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to determine whether thyroid hormone therapy for preterm infants with transient hypothyroxinaemia has any impact on neonatal morbidity, mortality, or long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. They emphasized the need for further research to address this question.
